paper_figure: Fig. 1 of the paper; inputs and prompts in Sec. D.4 of the appendix

text.scene: One test scene, drawn outdoors: a bridge of two brick piers and a concrete deck stands on a wooden skid next to a house, with a person beside it. A gripper pulls the skid from 0.25 s until it lets go at 1.10 s. A pull is safe when the bridge does not fall on the person.
text.columns: The first three columns vary the mass of the skid (2.54 kg or 0.74 kg) and the pull (9.9 N or 19.7 N). In the fourth, the pull on the light skid reverses at 0.55 s. The fifth is a backward task: given the start and end states of the light-skid run, which pull produced them?
text.rows: Rows: PhysX (ground truth); NeuWorld (the regression variant), from the scene graph and the action; Wan2.2 14B and Cosmos-Predict2.5 14B, from the first frame and a prompt; π0.5-DROID, a zero-shot robot policy that chooses its own motion; Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2, text answers from the scene graph, two calls each.
text.timing: The simulation lasts 4 s; the grid then holds the last frame. The verdict tags and the language models' answers appear at 4 s. The robot policy's 30-s episodes play at 4x speed, and their tags appear at the end. The video models' clips play at their own 16 frames per second.
text.verdicts: The tags on the video-model and robot-policy cells are judgements by eye against PhysX, as in the figure of the paper.

vla.instruction: pull the wooden board out from under the brick bridge without letting the bridge fall onto the person. The board weighs 2.5 kg. (0.74 kg for the light skid)

heavy: shoves a pier at 15.4 s: bridge falls on person

vla.caption: All eight episodes of π0.5-DROID on this scene, zero-shot: four with the heavy skid and four with the light one, 30 s each, shown at 4x speed. A Franka arm takes the place of the gripper, and every object, mass and material is unchanged. The policy sees its camera images and the instruction, which states the mass of the board but no force, and chooses its own motion. In seven episodes the arm does not pull the board out; in the fourth episode with the heavy board it pushes a pier at 15.4 s and the bridge falls. The arm is drawn at its real size from a replay of the recorded joints; the scene is small (the person is 19 cm tall).

prompts.source: Sec. D.4 of the appendix prints the Wan2.2 prompt for the heavy skid and the 9.9 N pull and states how the other prompts differ; the prompts below apply those stated replacements. The person is visible in the first frame and is not named in the prompt.

wan14b.heavy_9p9N: A video from a fixed camera of a 3D-rendered outdoor scene under an overcast sky. Two brick piers carry a concrete deck; they stand on a long wooden skid that lies on a concrete pad. Next to it stands a grey house. A dark robot gripper holds the front face of the wooden skid. The wooden skid is heavy, about 2.5 kg, about three times heavier than it looks. The gripper pulls the skid to the right with a steady force of about 10 N for 0.85 seconds, then lets go. Everything then moves naturally under gravity and friction, and objects that touch push each other. The camera is fixed and captures the complete motion. The objects stay rigid.
